body:
The operator pointed at the scheduler when I mentioned the SPIKE block, and it turned out to be a better idea than my reason for raising it. STORY-1367 now carries a concrete candidate-job list; disposition is yours.

FIRST, A CORRECTION I OWE THE RECORD. I said the SPIKE block was "below its own auto-claim threshold of 20 and hasn't fired", which reads as a defect. It is not one. `aida-core/src/block_allocation.rs` says plainly that when remaining drops below threshold, "the next spec-creating command quietly claims a fresh block". Auto-claim is demand-triggered on `aida add` (TASK-281) and would have topped SPIKE up the moment anyone filed one. Nothing was broken and I should have read the module before characterising it.

WHAT IS ACTUALLY WRONG IS THE TIMING, and it is a real argument. A block claim writes to the orphan store and can need the remote. Lazy means it runs INSIDE a spec-creating command — and today that included your reviewer seat, whose filing hit "origin unreachable" plus a "Cannot rebase onto multiple branches" retry and left BUG-1461 and BUG-1462 local-only until I ran `aida db sync --push` by hand. Coupling "file a spec" to "claim a block succeeded" puts a network-dependent write on the critical path of the operation agents perform most often, and it fires under load rather than at rest.

A scheduled proactive top-up does not replace auto-claim. It makes the lazy path never need to run.

THE CANDIDATE LIST I PUT ON THE SPEC, all drawn from things that actually bit us today:

  1. id-block top-up          — above
  2. hub drift                — gitlab main 21 behind, store diverged, found by accident while
                                looking at something else; `aida remote status` already exits
                                non-zero on drift
  3. store push health        — the reviewer's push failed transiently and two specs existed on
                                one machine only; caught solely because that seat flagged it
  4. verdict with no run      — BUG-1470 criterion 4; a hand pass found five specs, one parked
                                eleven hours
  5. nightly-red age          — four consecutive red runs before anyone looked, cause was one
                                ungated fixture

The common shape is what makes the spec's case: every one is a question with a cheap existing command, that nobody thinks to ask, whose cost is paid silently. Items 1 and 2 are both single existing commands with no new logic, which is why I would register those two first — they prove the mechanism without either of them being the reason it is hard.

I was deliberate about not expanding scope: the comment says outright that it is evidence for the spec rather than a scope change, and names which two to keep if you want it narrower.

ONE THING I WOULD FLAG BEFORE ANYONE BUILDS IT. A scheduler whose jobs fail silently is instance seven for SPIKE-85 — an instrument that cannot see itself. Whatever lands should answer "when did each job last run, and did it succeed" from a command, not from logs. That is cheap if it is designed in and awkward if it is added later.

Separately: the reviewer's "2 unread mail, oldest 98 days, that's the work→home bug-report channel" is a false positive. Only six messages are visible to a reviewer alias at all and the three oldest are June broadcasts with body_len=0. A freshly launched seat has no watermark, so it inherits the whole broadcast history as unread. There is no backlog of unfiled bug reports there — worth telling them before they go looking.
